title: Your CV Is Not a Job History. It Is a Sales Document.
excerpt: Most CVs accurately describe the past and persuade nobody. Here is what to change, line by line.
content:
Most CVs I am sent read like a police statement. They describe, accurately and in order, everything the person did. Job title, dates, list of duties, next job, repeat. Everything on the page is true. And almost none of it persuades anybody of anything.

The mistake sits in the first assumption. People treat the CV as a record of the past. It is not. It is an argument about the future, written in evidence from the past. Once that clicks, most of the other problems fix themselves.

Duties describe the role. Results describe you.

Here is a line I see constantly:

Responsible for managing the company’s social media accounts.

Every person who has ever held that job could write that sentence. It tells a recruiter what the role was, and nothing about whether you were good at it. It is a job description, not a claim.

Now the same work, rewritten as evidence:

Grew the company’s Instagram following from 2,000 to 47,000 in fourteen months, which became the source of roughly a third of inbound enquiries.

Same job. Completely different signal. The second version tells the reader what happens to a business when you are in the building.

The three questions every line should survive

Go through your CV line by line and ask:

  1. Could a mediocre person in this exact role write this same sentence? If yes, it is a duty. Rewrite it or delete it.
  2. Is there a number in it? Not every line needs one, but a CV with no numbers anywhere reads like opinion.
  3. Does it connect to something the business cares about? Revenue, cost, time, risk, or customers. Work that connects to none of these is hard to value.

People often protest that their work cannot be measured. It usually can, once you stop looking for a formal metric and start looking for the before and after. How long did it take before you, and after? How many mistakes? How many people did it serve? You are not fabricating data. You are noticing what you already changed.

Write for the machine, then for the human

For most international roles, software reads your CV before a person does. That system is looking for the words in the job advert. It does not understand that your Nigerian job title means the same thing as their British one.

So mirror their language. If the advert says stakeholder management and you called it client relations, use their phrase where it is honest to do so. This is not gaming the system. It is translation. You are removing a barrier that exists only because two organisations named the same work differently.

Then remember the human who reads it next. Keep it to two pages. Use a plain, readable font. Skip the photo, the date of birth, and the marital status, all of which are normal in Nigeria and read as strange or legally awkward in the UK, US and Canada.

Give unfamiliar things a scale

A recruiter in Manchester has no idea how large your former employer was, or how competitive your university is. What reads as impressive in Lagos can land as meaningless abroad, purely because the reader has no reference point.

Fix it with a short clause. Not a paragraph of explanation, just enough scale:

  • Instead of the company name alone, write the name followed by what it does and how big it is.
  • Instead of the university alone, add a line on selectivity or ranking if it genuinely helps.
  • Convert money to a currency the reader thinks in, or give both.

You are not apologising for where you worked. You are handing the reader a ruler so they can measure it properly.

One CV per application

The single CV sent to forty companies is the most common strategy and the least effective one. It has to be vague enough to fit everything, which means it is compelling for nothing.

You do not need to rewrite it each time. Keep one master document with everything you have ever done, then cut it down for each role, leading with whatever that employer actually asked for. Ten tailored applications will beat forty generic ones, and take less of your life.

Your CV has one job: to make a busy stranger believe you will be useful to them. Every line either does that work or takes up space that could.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
